# Lists, dictionaries, and the genetic code

Chapter 5 left you holding arithmetic. Bases 114 to 5,705 of `NM_007294.4` are
5,592 bases, which is 1,864 codons, which is 1,863 amino acids and one stop. The
protein those bases spell out is already sitting in NCBI as `NP_009225.1`, and
you've never made it yourself. Between the two sits the genetic code, a lookup
table with 64 rows. So what is a lookup table, to Python?

<!-- nlr-allow: 1864 -->

## What a list is good for

Three codons in the standard genetic code mean stop. They're `TAA`, `TAG` and
`TGA`, and nothing else about them matters yet. Put them in a list and look at
what a list gives you.

```{python}
stop_codons = ["TAA", "TAG", "TGA"]
print(len(stop_codons), "TGA" in stop_codons, "TGG" in stop_codons)
```

Square brackets, values separated by commas, and the order you typed stays the
order you get. A [list]{.term def="An ordered run of values. You reach a value
by its position, counting from zero."} is an ordered run of values, and you
reach one by its position counting from zero, so `stop_codons[0]` is `"TAA"`.
The `in` operator asks one question: is this value anywhere in the list? `TGA`
is a stop codon. `TGG` is tryptophan, one letter away, and the answer comes back
`False`.

Now try to hold the whole genetic code the same way. A codon on its own isn't
enough, because each entry has to carry the codon and what it codes for. So each
entry becomes a small list of two.

```{python}
pairs = [["TTT", "F"], ["TTC", "F"], ["TTA", "L"], ["TTG", "L"]]

for codon, amino_acid in pairs:
    if codon == "TTG":
        print(amino_acid)
```

Read that loop as a search. It walks the entries in order and prints when it
reaches the one whose first item is `TTG`. Four entries is cheap. Put all 64
codons in there and translate this gene, and you run that search 1,864 times. On
a sequence this short you'll never see the cost in the clock.

The expensive part is elsewhere. You wrote a search, and what you wanted was a
question.

## A dictionary answers instead of searching

Same four codons, written the way you meant them.

```{python}
four_codons = {"TTT": "F", "TTC": "F", "TTA": "L", "TTG": "L"}
print(four_codons["TTG"])
```

Curly braces this time, and each entry is a key, a colon, then a value. A
[dictionary]{.term def="A set of key and value pairs. You fetch a value by
naming its key rather than by its position."} is a set of key and value pairs,
and you get a value out by naming its key. `four_codons["TTG"]` isn't position
three of anything. It's the question "what does TTG code for" written down.

Keys and values behave differently, and that difference is the whole chapter. A
key appears once. Ask for `TTG` and you get one answer, or the dictionary raises
an error. Values repeat as often as they like, so `four_codons` has four keys
and two distinct values, because `TTT` and `TTC` both code for phenylalanine.

Python didn't invent that lopsidedness. The genetic code has it. Sixty-four
codons across twenty amino acids means most amino acids own several codons. So
codon to amino acid is a question with one answer, and amino acid to codon
isn't. You can translate DNA into protein. You can't run that backwards and
recover the DNA you started from, and no software will ever fix it for you.

## Sixty-four keys, twenty-one answers

You could type all 64 rows out by hand. Don't. A codon table typed from memory
is 64 chances to get a row wrong. One wrong row puts a wrong letter at every
place that codon appears, buried in 1,863 characters you were never going to
read. Nothing errors. Nothing looks odd.

The book ships the table as a file instead, generated from NCBI translation
table 1. That's the code your nuclear genes use. Mitochondria use different
codes, and so do a few single-celled groups. NCBI numbers each one separately on
the page this table came from. Here are the first rows of the file.

``` {.default filename="data/codon_table_standard.tsv"}
codon	amino_acid	name	is_start
TTT	F	Phenylalanine	no
TTC	F	Phenylalanine	no
TTA	L	Leucine	no
TTG	L	Leucine	yes
```

Four columns, separated by tabs: the codon, its amino acid as a one-letter code,
the full name, and a flag. Look at the flag on `TTG`. NCBI's note on table 1
says the standard code allows initiation from `TTG` and `CTG` as well as `ATG`,
so three codons in the file carry a `yes`. Chapter 12 looked for `ATG` and
nothing else, and this chapter keeps that decision.

Load the file into a dictionary. `open(...)` is the same borrowed line Chapter
12 used to read the sequence file. Read it as "hand me the contents of this
file" and leave it there. You'll meet `open` for real in Chapter 15.

```{python}
table_lines = open("data/codon_table_standard.tsv").read().splitlines()

codon_table = {}
for line in table_lines[1:]:
    codon, amino_acid, name, is_start = line.split("\t")
    codon_table[codon] = amino_acid

print(len(codon_table), codon_table["ATG"], codon_table["TGA"])
```

`table_lines[1:]` skips the header row, which is the slice you met in Chapter
11. Each line splits on its tabs into four pieces, and the loop keeps the first
two: the codon becomes a key, its amino acid becomes the value. `name` and
`is_start` get read and dropped.

So `codon_table` holds 64 keys. `ATG` is `M`, methionine. `TGA` is `*`, the
character translation software writes where a stop codon sits, and it means the
ribosome stops rather than adding anything.

Count how many codons each amino acid gets, to see how the 64 spread out.

```{python}
counts = {}
for amino_acid in codon_table.values():
    counts[amino_acid] = counts.get(amino_acid, 0) + 1

print(len(counts))
print(counts["L"], counts["S"], counts["R"], counts["M"], counts["W"])
```

`codon_table.values()` hands you the 64 values with the keys left behind.
`counts.get(amino_acid, 0)` looks an amino acid up and returns 0 if it isn't
there yet, which saves you checking first. That's the counting pattern this book
uses, and Chapter 20 runs it on a much bigger table.

Twenty-one outcomes: 20 amino acids and the stop. Leucine, serine and arginine
get six codons each. Methionine and tryptophan get one each. That spread is what
redundancy means in the genetic code, and it has a consequence you can measure
right now.

Take a codon and change one base. Three positions, three other bases at each,
so nine neighbors. Count how many of the nine leave the amino acid alone, and
how many turn the codon into a stop.

```{python}
for codon in ["CTG", "TGG"]:
    silent = 0
    stops = 0
    for position in range(3):
        for base in "ACGT":
            neighbor = codon[:position] + base + codon[position + 1:]
            if base != codon[position]:
                if codon_table[neighbor] == codon_table[codon]:
                    silent += 1
                if codon_table[neighbor] == "*":
                    stops += 1
    print(codon, codon_table[codon], silent, stops)
```

`CTG` is one of leucine's six codons. Four of its nine neighbors are still
leucine, and none of them is a stop. `TGG` is the only codon tryptophan has. Not
one of its nine neighbors is still tryptophan, and two of them end the protein
on the spot.

::: {.why}
This is what you're reading past when a paper reports that a variant changes one
base. In a leucine codon like `CTG`, four of the nine single-base changes leave
the protein exactly as it was. In the tryptophan codon, all nine change the
protein and two of them cut it short. The phrase "a single base change" covers
both, and the codon it landed in decides which one you're looking at.
:::

## Walkthrough: translating BRCA1

You finished Chapter 12 with the whole human transcript in `brca1`. Colab throws
your variables away when the runtime disconnects, so here's that same cell
again, unchanged.

```{python}
text = open("data/sequences/brca1_five_species.fasta").read()
lines = text.split(">")[1].splitlines()
brca1 = "".join(lines[1:])
print(len(brca1))
```

Now cut out the coding part. You read the range off the record back in Chapter
5: bases 114 to 5,705. Those are 1-based positions counting the first base as
base 1, and Python counts from zero, so base 114 sits at index 113. The far end
needs no adjustment at all. A Python slice stops before the index you hand it,
so 5705 takes you through base 5,705 and no further.

```{python}
coding = brca1[113:5705]
print(len(coding), len(coding) / 3)
```

Look at the `.0` on the end of that second number. 5,592 divides by three with
nothing left over. A coding sequence that doesn't divide by three is either
mis-annotated or mis-sliced, and this is the cheapest place to catch it.

Translate it. Step through `coding` three bases at a time and look up each
codon.

```{python}
translated = ""
for i in range(0, len(coding), 3):
    translated += codon_table[coding[i:i + 3]]

print(len(translated), translated.count("*"), translated[-1])
```

`range(0, len(coding), 3)` counts 0, 3, 6 and onwards to the end, so
`coding[i:i + 3]` is exactly one codon each time round the loop.

::: {.check}
Your output should read `1864 1 *`. That's 1,864 codons, one stop, and the stop
is the last character. More than one stop means your slice started in the wrong
place, so every codon after it is shifted. A last character that isn't `*` means
the slice ended in the wrong place. Either way, check both numbers in
`brca1[113:5705]` before you go on.
:::

```{python}
protein = translated[:-1]
print(len(protein))
print(protein[:9])
```

`translated[:-1]` drops the last character. A stop codon isn't an amino acid, so
it has no place in a protein sequence. That leaves 1,863 residues, which is
exactly the length `NP_009225.1` reports, and the first nine of them are
`MDLSALRVE`. Exercise 13.2 checks the rest.

One number here you can check against work you've already done. Back in Chapter
12 you stepped through this coding sequence in threes and found 30 in-frame
`ATG`s. Every `ATG` the ribosome reads as a word puts a methionine into the
protein, so the letter `M` should turn up 30 times.

```{python}
print(protein.count("M"))
```

Two routes, two different pieces of code, one answer. Agreement between
independent routes is the best evidence you can get with nobody to ask.

### The strand you didn't translate

You made one more decision than you noticed. `coding` came out of a RefSeq mRNA,
which is already the strand and the direction that gets read. Try the other one
and watch what comes back.

```{python}
pairing = {"A": "T", "C": "G", "G": "C", "T": "A"}

other_strand = ""
for base in reversed(coding):
    other_strand += pairing[base]

wrong = ""
for i in range(0, len(other_strand), 3):
    wrong += codon_table[other_strand[i:i + 3]]

print(wrong[:20], wrong.count("*"), wrong.find("*"))
```

`pairing` is a dictionary too, four keys wide, and it's the base-pairing rule
written down as a lookup. `reversed()` walks a string backwards. Together they
hand you the complementary strand read the way a ribosome would read it.
Translating that gives you 67 residues before the first stop turns up, and 93
stops once you count the whole thing.

::: {.trap}
Any stretch of DNA has two strands and three reading frames on each, so six ways
to translate it. Only one of them gave you `NP_009225.1`. All six produce
letters, so the output looks equally healthy whichever one you're in. The wrong
strand here handed back a clean run of 67 residues before its first stop and
warned you about nothing. The fix in this chapter is one sentence: a RefSeq mRNA
like `NM_007294.4` is already the strand that gets translated, so translate it
exactly as it arrives. Sequence taken straight off a chromosome for a
minus-strand gene like *BRCA1* has to be flipped first, and Chapter 17 gives you
a one-line way to do the flip.
:::

## Exercises

Solutions are in the book's repository under `scripts/solutions/`. Work the
exercise first.

::: {.exercise num="13.1" time="45 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Write a translator that turns any coding sequence into a protein sequence, then
run it on something shorter than *BRCA1* to prove it isn't hard-wired to one
gene.
:::
::: {.given}
A DNA string in uppercase `A`, `C`, `G` and `T` whose length divides by three,
plus the `codon_table` dictionary you built above.
:::
::: {.produce}
One string of one-letter amino acid codes, with `*` for each stop, and two
numbers: how long the string is and how many stops it contains.
:::
::: {.check}
Write down the length you expect before you run anything. On `coding` you should
get 1,864 characters with one `*` at the end. On `coding[:30]`, the first 30
bases, you should get 10 characters, `MDLSALRVEE`, and no `*` at all. If your
translator throws the stop away for you, that's a decision you made, and
Exercise 13.2 will make you undo it.
:::

::: {.answerbox height="1.8in"}
:::
:::

::: {.exercise num="13.2" time="30 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Check your protein against the one NCBI deposited, character by character.
:::
::: {.given}
`NP_009225.1`, the protein record linked from `NM_007294.4`. Take the sequence
in FASTA. It arrives wrapped across many lines, so drop the header and join the
lines before you compare anything.
:::
::: {.produce}
Three values: the length of your protein, the length of NCBI's, and whether the
two strings are equal.
:::
::: {.check}
1,863, 1,863 and `True`. If you got 1,864 residues you kept the stop codon, and
NCBI doesn't. If yours is much shorter you started at base 1 instead of base 114
and ran into a stop out in the untranslated part after 59 residues. If the two
lengths agree and the strings don't, print the first position where they differ
and go and look at the codon that produced it.
:::

::: {.answerbox height="1.8in"}
:::
:::

That second exercise puts an outside authority on your code. You're reproducing
a deposited protein from a deposited transcript, with a table you loaded and a
loop you wrote. Either the strings match or they don't, and a string comparison
gives no partial credit.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the live NCBI interface on 2 August 2026. `NP_009225.1` is
reachable from the `NM_007294.4` record, and the protein record offers its
sequence in FASTA. NCBI has moved and relabeled that link before, so look for
the format name rather than for a button in a fixed place.
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="KeyError: 'CA'"}
Python is talking, and it's the dictionary complaining. Every key in
`codon_table` is three letters long. `CA` is two, so you ran off the end of a
sequence whose length doesn't divide by three. The usual cause is translating
the whole 7,088-base transcript instead of the 5,592-base coding part. Slice
bases 114 to 5,705 out first.
:::

::: {.errfix err="KeyError: 'atg'"}
Same dictionary, different cause. Your sequence is lowercase and the keys are
uppercase, and Python compares text exactly. You met lowercase sequence back in
Chapter 11, along with what it costs you. Call `.upper()` on the sequence before
you translate it.
:::

::: {.errfix err="ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 4, got 1)"}
Python is talking, and it's talking about the line that splits the file. You
asked for four pieces and one came back, so the split found nothing to split on.
The codon table is separated by tabs rather than commas, and a tab inside quotes
is written `\t`. Check that character before you check anything else.
:::

::: {.errfix err="FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data/codon_table_standard.tsv'"}
Python is talking, and it looked in the folder it's running from. That's the
same folder Chapter 12 opened the sequence file from, so if that worked and this
doesn't, you're in a new session or a different folder. Chapter 15 covers where
a notebook looks and how to point it somewhere else.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Say what a list answers well and what a dictionary answers well, using the
  genetic code as the example
- Build a dictionary from a file and check that it holds 64 keys
- Count the codons per amino acid, and name the two amino acids that have one
  codon each
- Translate a coding sequence and say why you drop the last character
- Check a protein you translated against a deposited one, and name two ways the
  two lengths can disagree
- Say why translation runs in one direction only
:::
